analysis.one_liner: Established a government-run universal health insurance program with no premiums, deductibles, or copays.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in four House committees from March 1999 until the Congress ended, with 21 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health coverage, and most private health insurance with a single public program run by the states under federal standards. Every US resident would get a health security card covering hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, and long-term care, with no deductibles or copays for acute care. It would be financed by a new payroll tax on employers, a new income tax, and higher tobacco taxes, and would give a national board power to set drug prices and hospital budgets.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone without coverage or with inadequate coverage: about 40 million Americans were uninsured in 1999, and millions more faced deductibles, copays, and premium costs that the bill eliminated. People with preexisting conditions, people who lost jobs, and families paying out of pocket for drugs, dental, and long-term care would all have gained guaranteed coverage they kept regardless of employment or state of residence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and everyone paying premiums

how_it_helps.text: Every US citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be entitled to comprehensive coverage from January 1, 2001, with automatic enrollment at birth or immigration.
The bill prohibits deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments for acute and preventive care, and bars providers from balance-billing patients for covered services.

Benefits would cover outpatient prescription drugs at board-set maximum prices, dental care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, hospice, and home and community-based long-term care — services many current plans exclude.
Coverage would be portable across states, would supersede Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, and CHAMPUS, and states could not impose waiting periods longer than three months.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the self-employed would pay a new health care payroll excise tax; individuals would pay a new health care income tax; tobacco users would pay higher excise taxes. Health insurers would lose the core business of duplicative coverage, which the bill prohibits. Pharmaceutical makers would face board-set maximum drug prices, and hospitals would operate under approved global budgets instead of billing per service.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, high earners, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The financing would be a large, visible new tax burden: a payroll excise tax on every employer and the self-employed, a new individual health care income tax with no credits allowed, and higher tobacco taxes.

The bill prohibits the sale of private insurance that duplicates covered benefits, eliminating the private insurance product line entirely in participating states and ending the employer-based coverage system most workers then relied on.

An appointed federal board would set national and state budgets, approved drug lists with maximum prices, and payment methods, concentrating substantial pricing and coverage decisions in a new federal body and requiring a massive transition away from Medicare, Medicaid, and employer plans.

Long-term care would carry cost-sharing — 20 percent coinsurance for home and community-based services and 35 percent for nursing facility services — for people above 100-200 percent of the poverty line.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — universal coverage with no cost-sharing for acute care, covering services most plans exclude — was broad and would have ended medical debt and coverage loss tied to jobs. The cost was equally real: new taxes on employers and income large enough to replace all existing public and private health spending, the elimination of private duplicate coverage, and a heavy administrative transition to state-run programs with global hospital budgets and board-set drug prices. Critics could fairly argue the funding and budgeting mechanisms were untested at that scale; supporters answered that they were the mechanism for containing costs. The bill was never debated on the merits in any committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees in March 1999 and then to subcommittees, and none of them ever produced a bill or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on March 18, 1999, with original cosponsors including Reps. Conyers, Sanders, Nadler, Hinchey, Serrano, Fattah, Olver, and Coyne.
It was referred to the Committees on Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services — a four-way referral that required each committee to act on the portions under its jurisdiction.
In April 1999 it was referred to subcommittees: Civil Service, Health, Military Personnel, and Health and Environment.
No committee reported the bill, no markup was scheduled, and no floor vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors — 20 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican support appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: insurers, drug makers, and employers kept the existing employer-based, multi-payer system without the new payroll tax, income tax, drug price controls, or global hospital budgets the bill would have imposed. The uninsured and underinsured remained where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing insurance industry and employers

industries.note: The bill bans the sale of insurance duplicating program benefits and supersedes Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee coverage, effectively ending the private health insurance business in participating states. Its elimination is the mechanism by which premiums, deductibles, and claim denials disappear for the public.
A national board would establish an approved drug list and set maximum prices, ending the industry's pricing power over the entire American market.
Employers would pay a new payroll excise tax, but would stop paying rising private health premiums and exit the business of providing health benefits, which ERISA amendments would formalize.

Facilities would receive guaranteed payment for all patients instead of uncompensated care, but under approved global operating budgets rather than per-service billing — trading billing freedom for payment security and cost control.
Excise taxes on tobacco products would rise to help fund the program; higher prices reduce smoking, which is a public health gain.
